2005-2007

August 2005
PREFACE
In late 2003 and early 2004, the United Nations Country Team for Iraq (UNCT) prepared a strategic plan called A Strategy for Assistance to Iraq covering the period 2004 – 2006, but specifically focusing on 200This was endorsed at the International Donors Conference at Abu Dhabi on 28-29 February 200As a document it was primarily based on the Needs Assessment jointly prepared by the UN and the World Bank in mid-2003 and endorsed by the International Donors Conference on the Reconstruction of Iraq (Madrid: 23-24 October, 2003).The UN’s overarching objective at that time was, and indeed continues to be, to help the people of Iraq. The underlying vision was for a peaceful transition, strongly underscored by transparent, credible and trust-building processes, to a unified Iraq that has full sovereignty, that is democratic, respects human rights and the rule of law, encourages inspirational leadership to face the challenges of nationwide reconciliation, reconstruction, and development, and draws on the wealth of Iraqi and external human, social and natural capital at its disposal to achieve its full potential in peaceful harmony with the region and the world. For its part the UNCT adopted a “cluster approach” and restructured operations into originally ten, now eleven, clusters of agencies based on commonality of focus and comparative advantage. Many significant changes and developments took place in 2004, not least of which were the return of sovereignty to Iraqis (28 June), the issuing of UN Security Council Resolution 1546 (8 June), and the publication of the Iraqi-owned National Development Strategy 2005 – 2007 (NDS) on 13 October, amongst other. Hence, there was clearly a need for the UNCT to re-visit its strategic plan to assess how relevant and effective various programmes and operational arrangements were in 2004, and from the lessons learned to date, to decide on how best to align the UN’s strategic response with the NDS and the circumstances on the ground – both prevailing and anticipated.
This new document first and foremost builds on the NDS, and on cluster and agency contributions, inputs from consultancies and ongoing and widespread consultations between clusters agencies and their respective line ministries and government counterparts. A range of data sources were used - the 2004 version of this document, the 2003 joint UN/WB Needs Assessment; the UNCT Strategic Plan for IDPs in Iraq; World Bank reports, and on individual  references such as the Brookings Institute “Iraq Index Tracking Variables of Reconstruction & Security in Post-Saddam Hussein Iraq”;. The main aim of this document it to update the previous UN Assistance Strategy based on analyses of lessons learned over the past year, new county data (WFP Baseline Survey; the Ministry of Health report – Health in Iraq – September 2004; the Ministry of Education Report - Educational Statistics in Iraq Volume 1 - October 2004 and Ministry of Education [in collaboration with UNICEF] Educational Statistics in Iraq Volume 2 Analytical report - December 2004) not then available and to reflect the Iraqi platform for reform outlined at the Donors’ Committee meeting held in Tokyo, 13-14 October, 2004.
In keeping with the UN’s core values this document has been written from a rights-based perspective on sustainable human development within the framework provided by the Millennium Declaration, Global Conferences, and Conventions. In this perspective, development is not confined to the economic spectrum only, but entails a much broader vision related to the achievement of the five categories of human rights: civil, cultural, economic, political and social which are inextricably linked. That is why this revised document highlights the poverty situation from a social, economic, governance and human rights perspective and defines common responses based on the implications of this concept of sustainable human development. It is going to be used as a framework for promoting more equitable and sustainable human development in Iraq, and also reflect closely the UNAMI mandate as outlined in UN Security Council Resolution 1546: clause 7 (b). As with any strategic planning instrument of this nature, this document must continue to be considered a “work-in-progress”.  A more comprehensive programming document representing fuller details of UN assistance to Iraq, after consultation with all stakeholders (government, donors, other multi-lateral organisations and partners) on the content of this strategy with eventual endorsement by the Government, is envisioned for release by the end of February 2005.

Lessons Learned
The major lesson learned in relation to the implementation of planned UN programmes and projects was the underestimation of the duration and tenacity of post-war conflict and the sophistication which those involved in the conflict were able to employ.  Coupled with this was the underestimation of how the protracted conflict would affect the broader Iraqi population and therefore UN operations in country.
Security conditions continue to limit how much the UN can deliver for the time being; therefore the level of threat to UN staff is likely to remain very high for the foreseeable future, forcing the UN to keep its international presence to a minimum. The Security Council acknowledged those limits by using the words “as circumstances permit” in the SC resolution 1546.
The August 2003 bombing, and the attack on the International Committee of the Red Cross, put an end to business as usual and opened a new chapter for the United Nations. The UN must reinforce its security measures.  But this is not only a question of more equipment, more guards, or more protective film on windows, important as such steps are.  The UN also needs to rethink how it operates.  If it is to reduce exposure in situations of high risk, it must be ready to work in an integrated fashion, as a full team.
The Cluster System was born of this need to work in an integrated fashion.  Although the cluster approach for Iraq is still a work-in-progress, it has the potential to become a key UN system reform, or at least a benchmark for similar reforms. Due to the complexity of the enterprise, as a reform it is still fragile.  Therefore, a key learning process during 2004 for UN agencies working in Iraq was realisation of the strengths and weaknesses of instituting such a reform and the impact it had on implementation of programmes.  We therefore need to grasp the opportunity to develop this concept further and demonstrate that the UN system and its constituent agencies as a learning organisation have the courage to institute credible reform.  To that end, one of the first activities for the UNCT in 2005 is to examine ways and means to make the cluster system more effective and efficient in delivering what is required for the Iraqi people. The cluster system was effective in enabling agencies to work together, understand each other’s strengths and weaknesses and focus on sector development across eleven clusters.  However, in the future the UN should establish processes that do not elicit a conflict of interest between agencies.  As the cluster system is required to operate outside the country, the need has become more urgent to think about alternatives, perhaps the establishment of a combined system, part working inside the country, and part outside the country, with the view of bringing all activities inside.  Many Iraqis demand that all activities of the UN and other international organizations move to Iraq with due consideration of the security environment.
As well as reforming the cluster approach in making delivery of interventions more streamlined, the UN also needs to understand that the current conflict in Iraq is not a new phenomenon, but the most serious contemporary manifestation of a chronic crisis of governance caused by persistent patterns of economic, social and political exploitation formed over many years. The frontiers that came to define Iraq were drawn up little understanding of local sensibilities and had inevitable consequences for regional rivalries and spheres of sovereignty that have so far persisted for nearly eighty years.  
The longer term political history of Iraq can be characterised as a turbulent process of exploitation, competition, sectarianism and inter-clan disputes involving, outside powers, powerful groups of sheiks and landowners and religious interests. The communities and interest groups that make up the modern state of Iraq are bound together by centuries of economic interaction, much of it exploitative. Religion and ideologies of ethnicity have emerged, more sharply in some periods, as factors that define access to social, political and legal rights – a cultural determinant even exploited by the so called sectarian regime of Saddam Hussein.   
This background can in some part explain the lack of current institutional capacity to coordinate developmental efforts toward reconstruction.  Another key lesson learned by the UN therefore, during 2004, was the overestimation of the reliability of internal coordination mechanisms and capacity generally to support and enable broad-based reconstruction activities.  In addition donors also were not effective in coordinating the aid efforts and subsequently many activities were taking place in tandem that could have been more effective if related to like designed programmes or programmes covering the same sector needs.  
Linked to the lack of institutional capacity is the lack of resources available to Iraqi authorities across all ministries on all levels.  All ministries experience a dearth of appropriate people, material, institutional and financial resources to enable reconstruction and rehabilitation to take place at the rate expected or needed.  This therefore does not provide an environment conducive to sustainability for programmes implemented by the United Nations.  Coupled with governmental resource and capacity limitations sometimes negatively affecting UN implementation is the lack of institutional memory or knowledge within government manifested in changes in staff and government officials at the very senior or ministerial levels of government.  This has stifled on some occasions the continuity of programmes initiated by the UN to the extent that modification of implementation plans became necessary after work had begun to accommodate changes in policy direction.  However, some improvement has been realised more recently, on which the incoming Government will build upon. Nevertheless, the UN will boost assistance to develop the role of institutions and to establish new institutions during 2005 and beyond.
The UN team working for Iraq did not seek to engage in supporting government policy formulation during 2004 for varying reasons.  One, the need for more basic and urgent services and resources such as medicine, health facilities, education material, water and electricity took precedence.  In addition, many agencies and clusters believed it was premature to consider longer-term policy formulation support in light of the fact that an Interim Government was in place whose structure and focus could change dramatically in a post-elections Iraq. 
Furthermore, despite the promises of the varying military style governments of the past to introduce democracy the country was yet to see its first truly democratic general election in which all parts of the country are able to vote.  Hence, it would have been difficult to anticipate specific outcomes with the holding of the first elections held on 30 January 2005, since there is no reference point within Iraqi political history to indicate how this broad-based electoral process would affect and colour the political landscape of the future. Therefore, the UN will be ready in 2005 to assist and support the Transitional Government of Iraq when and if required to shape the new political environment towards forming a new society. 
To summarise, the lessons of 2003/2004 have taught the UN that the overly optimistic expectations of what was possible as far as reconstruction in Iraq by all stakeholders should be tapered to a more cautiously optimistic level by focusing efforts strategically to those areas that can produce the greatest results and benefits for the people of Iraq.  There also needs to be a better awareness of Iraq’s capacity, resources and political will to implement reform and sustain interventions made on their behalf by the UN and other benefactors.   Finally, there is a need for international actors in Iraq to better coordinate their aid efforts as well as develop a wider awareness of the historical, political economic nature of the on-going conflict that is manifested in the increase in criminal activity for whatever reason and purpose and the rise of insurrectionary groups and activities. 
In conclusion expectations in a crisis/post-crisis situation on all levels of reconstruction and reform need to be moderated and based on a realistic understanding of the long-term social, economic and political dynamics affecting lives and livelihoods of the various peoples of Iraq.  Hence, the UN strategic focus outlined in this document will aim at being driven by Iraqi realities rather than by ideological prerogatives.
Current Context
Introduction
Iraq is a highly multi-cultural society with a current approximate 27 million inhabitants. Three wars over two decades, the rule of a divisive dictatorial regime and years of sanctions isolating the country have had a devastating impact on Iraq’s people. Consequently, human rights were violated, infrastructure became dilapidated and the economy and social services severely eroded. Negative economic growth is believed to exist in most places, but not necessarily throughout the country as the range of activities and investment in the north of the country demonstrate. Years of war, war reparations, sanctions and Iraq’s large external debt burden also diverted scarce financial and human resources away from development. The widespread lack of equitable and sound investment in development under the previous regime led to a reluctance by the international community to offer funding for development bi-laterally or multi-laterally until recently. Humanitarian relief from the donor community, though, continues for immediate emergency needs arising from the on-going conflict. Within this context, it is not surprising that poverty has sharply increased and is widespread. 
The destruction of the social and economic infrastructure of Iraq has severely disrupted industrial, agricultural and trading activity. Subsequently, many regions with rich potential for mineral exploitation and agricultural production are not able to adequately feed its inhabitants. The donor community has reacted to this situation by supporting live-saving humanitarian assistance and in addition the Iraqi authorities’ PDS (Public Distribution System) has helped meet the urgent survival needs of a population suffering from endemic conflict, exacerbated by a lack of good governance and quality institutions and thus limited access to basic services.  Approximately, 16 million people or 60% of the population are reliant upon the PDS in varying degrees for daily subsistence. Life-sustaining interventions therefore need to re-focus from reinforcing dependency mechanisms to strengthening coping mechanisms for vulnerable communities in order to lessen high rates of dependency. 
The destruction of the productive base and of infrastructure, the breakdown of social services, and difficulties caused by continuing conflict and depletion of resources will therefore take huge investments and long-term commitments (over generations) to redress. The assessment undertaken in 2003 jointly by the United Nations, the World Bank, with input from International Monetary Fund, covering 14 sectors estimated Iraq’s reconstruction needs to be in the order of US$36 billion for the period 2004-200 However this assessment may need to be revised upwards considering the continuing conflict and destruction in Iraq since the original analysis took place.
The most potent destruction however, is manifested in the disruption of the social and political fabric of Iraqi society. The social and political capital comprising of the country’s laws, institutions, culture and traditions, enabling overall governance of the country needs urgent attention if economic reform is to be implemented successfully.  If the structural and regulatory frameworks in which reform needs to take place do not exist, then the changes indicated within any proposed reform have nothing on which to graft. The institutions include the political, legal, judicial institutions and agencies, both public and private, civil society and others that are the ultimate source of authority and trust. Rebuilding and investing in the political and social capital is the major task of nation-building in post-conflict societies and economies. Solely rebuilding destroyed physical infrastructure will not restore the torn political and social fabric, nor diminish the probability of renewal of violence and conflict.
The elections that took place in January 2005 was a positive step forward creating hope, that can be built upon, in bringing finalisation to changes in the political process by the end of 2005. This major task will bring normalisation to the country.  Normalisation will bring stability, better law and order, more interaction with Iraq’s neighbours and the broader world community thus producing an environment more conducive to on-going reform needed at all levels in all sectors of development
Basic Social Services Development
In the case of Iraq what is needed is to contribute in creating a functional and sustainable society that caters for diversities in the communities creating opportunities to overcome poverty by establishing a minimum base line of standards of living and access to social services.  It is essential that the vulnerable and those most affected by previous policies receive attention and participate and contribute to the process. This is a particular focus of the UN.
In the area of basic services; access to and quality of health, housing, education, water supply and sanitation, and also to a degree, food, have all deteriorated after many years of neglect, with rural facilities especially being poorly staffed and equipped. Previous Government policy favoured a centralised approach and thus the development of basic social services in urban areas benefited, to the detriment of rural populations that make up the majority of the poor and vulnerable. Helping to correct this imbalance is a target of the UN’s interventions.
Low and irregularly paid salaries in the health and education sectors as well as other public utility organisations have led to an exodus of trained workers, for better opportunities overseas or in other more lucrative sectors in Iraq. A large number of well-educated Iraqis are currently working in other Gulf States as well as Europe, USA, Canada, Australia and New Zealand. In addition, the enormous requirements of the military machine during successive wars deprived public utility organisations of valuable financial, material and human resources. Together these factors, contribute to the deterioration of the quality of health, housing, education, water, sanitation, transport, telecommunications and electricity services and available expertise generally within the country. There has been an upward revision of public sector salaries across the board, which is feeding its way into the economy.  
With limited employment opportunities in the public sector, the development of the private sector has become imperative for employment generation. Micro and small home-based enterprises offer an important source of employment and income in both rural and urban areas. In view of Iraq’s potential income and its human resource base, it is appropriate to strengthen small and medium enterprises, as well as maximising labour-intensive enterprises in agriculture, construction, housing and other sectors, with policy advice and skills enhancement.
Good Governance and Human Security
Despite the prominence of civil society action in Iraq’s earlier modern political history following a series of military coups, civil society was afforded little power and therefore had little influence over government policy over the last few decades.  Although the current government is publicly supportive of action by the wider society, this needs to be manifested in promoting broad civil society debate expressing varied political views.  
The weakened public infrastructure and services, the departure of qualified people to other parts of the world in conjunction with the weak power base of regional authorities, combine to make development of an active civil society more difficult that in other countries, but not impossible. One concern is that the number of genuine non-governmental actors may remain small and their influence weak in the short- to medium-term, but time will tell.  Furthermore, the prevailing lack of institutional ability and law enforcement capacity within the current political environment reinforces the weak position of the general population in determining country direction.  
Iraq has ratified all the major international conventions in relation to human rights and, therefore, current and future governments should not only promote the principles underlying these conventions, but should seek to implement policies that uphold the conventions.  The challenge therefore for Iraq is to completely reform the socio-political structure and therefore many aspects of its legal, administrative and constitutional framework that has to date coloured the political landscape.
The human rights situation is poor particularly for minorities and women. Fundamental human rights such as the right to life and to physical integrity, the right to liberty and security have in the past been severely violated, particularly in relation to populations living directly in zones of conflict or in areas discriminated by previous Government policy due to religious or tribal orientations. Structural human rights issues need improvement and reform and awareness among the population of their constitutional and legal rights needs improvement. 
Good governance based on the rule-of-law and respect for human rights has a clear relationship with broad-based economic growth and a vibrant, empowered civil society, in that each facilitates and sustains the other. Commitment to capacity strengthening across all sectors is a key factor in making the relationship strong and lasting. Achievement of sustainable human development is dependent on progress on all the above three fronts as well as a cessation of the current conflict.  
A consequence of rising insurgency and aggression is that the institutional and administrative mechanisms available to regulate or control conflict do not function well, if at all. This may point to a need to establish programmes that address conflict resolution at grass-roots level that encompasses capacity building for local governance institutions and a framework for decentralisation and devolution of resources from the central government to the governorates. Conflict resolution activities not addressed downstream as well as upstream could render all other developmental or humanitarian interventions inoperable or at best unsustainable.  Current and future governments with support from the UN and other stakeholders can closely examine the causes and affects of conflict in Iraq in order to define how best to address the needs of people across varying regional imperatives.
A key challenge for any future government will be to strike a balance between emergency governance mechanisms including sequencing of the varying levels of reforms needed for institutional change and longer term work.  This is especially crucial considering that the UN as well as other international institutions is unable to undertake full operations in country due to the prevailing security conditions.  
The Economy and Poverty in Iraq
The Iraqi economy is predominantly based on mineral exploitation namely oil with some revenue coming from agriculture (about 10% of the total). However, environmental degradation and mismanagement of natural resources has decreased productivity. Conflict and declining productivity related to environmental degradation, poor storage facilities, dilapidated infrastructure and previous Government policy have led to economic instability, unemployment and food insecurity.  This coupled with the fact that the current Iraqi authorities are compelled to continue to subsidise the cost of water, electricity, fuel and food and other utilities up to the level of 90% of total costs, hampering the Government’s capacity to invest in sustainable future development of the country.  However, the phasing out or reduction of subsidies will need to be accompanied with the establishment of a social safety net structure supported by appropriate fiscal and legal structure and regulation to ensure stringent economic reform does not have dire consequences for the most vulnerable communities (acutely impoverished, IDPs, disadvantaged). In this regard the need for activating social safety nets as soon as possible is vital.
Industrial and agricultural development is also seriously hampered by a lack of access to finance, advisory services and technology and deficient institutional systems and regulatory frameworks. Coupled with this is the general neglect of environmental considerations in relation to industrial and agricultural development negatively affecting Iraqi livelihoods.  Furthermore, although there is a strong linkage between agriculture and industry, a small percentage of agricultural produce is processed in Iraq limiting scope for sustainable livelihoods.  With low productivity and minimal value adding activities, the opening up of the Iraqi economy, therefore, requires major improvements in the quality and competitiveness of businesses and major private sector investment that encourages diversification of the productive base of the country.
War has caused the collapse of the urban and rural economic infrastructure. Access to markets in areas of conflict is reduced and investment destroyed. Lack of opportunities for human development caused by conflict will undermine the ability of the local population to play a decisive role on the national stage or even be active citizens at a local level in the longer term. Civilian war-related and crime related deaths in the most recent war and continuing conflict in its aftermath is considered high over an eighteen month period. 
Conflict will always have a major impact on having the right mix of investment and human capital available for economic growth. At the same time as having a dearth of professional expertise available for reconstruction Iraq faces increased pressure to provide employment to a predominately young (under 25 years) growing population. Employment opportunities are scarce with up to approximately 30% of the workforce being unemployed according to the government, while youth face double this rate of unemployment. Not surprisingly, underemployment is also widespread. Urban-biased policies favoured by the previous regime and also the impact of ongoing conflict again are the root causes. 
Following the initial reconstruction phase, if the government commits to Millennium Development targets, includes new objectives based on MDGs (Millennium Development Goals) in long-term development planning and translates them into actual policy instruments for implementation in the field, the Iraqi people should be able to see significant improvements in their living conditions.
Fostering human development in Iraq requires a broader-based, equitable and environmentally sustainable economic growth, which raises the income level and living standards of the whole country, particularly the poor through, employment and higher productivity.  
The government is looking at taking a holistic approach to poverty alleviation and pro-poor growth strategies through a comprehensive national policy addressing employment, growth with equity, social services rehabilitation, and sustainable human resource development.  The root causes of poverty are complex and interrelated and therefore poverty has to be understood as a multi-dimensional phenomenon. A broad based poverty assessment and subsequent analysis should take into account the complexity, dynamics and interrelationships of the historical, socio-cultural, socio-economic and geo-political dimensions. The rights-based approach provides a coherent framework for such analysis. From this perspective, poverty is a condition characterised by serious deprivation of basic rights and needs in terms of food, nutrition, water, health, shelter, education, electricity, lack of access and availability of resources and a lack of institutional capacity to safeguard respect and promotion of rights and the opportunities to change the situation.  Furthermore, poverty is augmented by imbalanced policies, discrimination and inappropriate developmental schemes.
Poverty in Iraq is also closely related to the wars of the previous decades and the depravations caused by the sanctions following these wars. The burden of war falls on the whole community, however, especially heavily upon the poor and vulnerable, in particular women and children.  Conflict and the continuing insecurity remains a major threat to lasting peace and retreat from poverty and stumbling block for sustained reconstruction and development in Iraq. 
The UN developmental focus in Iraq	
Overview
The United Nations traditionally applies different responses according to the specific situation of a country in need. Emergency relief assistance is normally offered in a humanitarian crisis, whereas support for wider long-term development activities is offered in times of stability. However, crisis and stability can sometimes co-exist.  What is being observed is that the nature of emergency situations is changing in two fundamental respects.  First, emergencies appear to more prevalent. In parts of the world, crisis and instability are increasingly the norm where development is being crowded out.  Second, the parameters of an emergency are changing, in that it is no longer a singular event of short duration that temporarily interrupts the progress of development.  Rather, an emergency is increasingly a complex, multifaceted and protracted phenomenon that has a profound impact on social and economic development. The concept of development has to absorb this change and in doing so clarify what is meant by development for the country in turmoil. For its part UN country programming absorbed this shift and devised a model for strategic response specific to the unique situation in Iraq. 
The UN Country Team determined in its previous strategic plan (2004) that the conventional model - in which development follows rehabilitation follows emergency or humanitarian - was not appropriate for Iraq. The UNCT correctly ascertained that even in a protracted crisis such as that being experienced in Iraq, development cannot be postponed. It therefore adopted a modus operandi that introduced rehabilitation and development activities alongside its humanitarian activities, under a programme approach within the new cluster system. In essence the UNCT did not assume an end to the conflict or focus only on peaceful regions of the country, but rather took steps to deal with the basic needs of the population in as many areas as possible while paving the way for eventual development activities.  However, expectations of what is possible in this crisis/post-crisis situation needs to be based on a realistic understanding of the long-term social, economic and political dynamics affecting lives and livelihoods of the people of Iraq.  
Experience suggests that developmental interventions requires a transition phase, which may be a necessary prerequisite for widespread and longer term development, specifically covering the promotion of security, easing of social conflict and tensions, meeting basic needs, key institutional strengthening and capacity building. In this transition stage the UN, in addition to adopting a needs-based approach for its humanitarian operations, attempts to promote greater security through rights-based programming that addresses advocacy and development of good governance and conflict resolution at all levels. There is little doubt that there is a clear relationship between underdevelopment (demonstrated by the level and distribution of poverty including under-employment and unemployment) and conflict in Iraq, and this has a strong underlying social exclusion dimension arising from previous periods in Iraq’s recent history.  In this context, the UN support to restoring security in the country will continue to address the causes of conflict and help bring about a national polity based on democracy and mutual respect. Failure to properly address the sources of the conflict, such as isolationism, exploitation, resource access and democratic accountability only postpones the inevitability of future conflict. 
This document is a strategic framework linking the emergency/humanitarian, rehabilitation and development (including response to political, institutional and societal needs) dimensions of aid for people-centred development and as such has the following targets:
To give both clear direction and coordination to all UN activities in Iraq - emergency/humanitarian, rehabilitation and developmental, and to promote effectiveness, efficiency and accountability in the utilisation of assets and resources.
To pave the way for the gradual transformation from humanitarian relief operations and highly subsidised government interventions covering food, water, electricity, fuel, etc. to rehabilitation and development programmes and encourage prioritised assistance that is relevant, life-enhancing, and targeted.
To promote and guide UN advocacy for security, the rule-of-law and human rights in Iraq.
The Role of Partnerships
The realisation of a people-centred development framework implemented through the cluster system, adopting a programme approach with shared objectives and multi-sectoral strategies, requires a broader partnership framework including resident and non-resident UN Agencies, Government, donors, civil society and the private sector. Building on the work with partners to date, strengthening partnerships will encourage greater exchange of information, experiences and best practices.  This should continue to add significant value to future policy-making and programme formulation by way of a virtuous circle.  Adopting a joint effort toward building and sharing a knowledge base of Iraq’s evolving situation should increase the UN system’s effectiveness further in assisting the people of Iraq.  Programme execution, implementation and resource mobilisation in the field shall be better co-ordinated to obtain a greater rate of success as the UNCT continues to bring all its efforts together under an umbrella approach.  
It is now perhaps time to give priority to national execution modalities in order to implement successfully programmes supported by the UN.  The current security environment makes direct execution difficult. National execution therefore may be an alternative strategy for UN engagement and implementation of activities. Since many UN agencies cannot be present in-country in the normal sense of a UN country operation, ministries, NGO’s, and the private sector should play a more prominent role with agencies playing a role from outside the country in order that development in the country is not delayed further. One key lesson learned by the IIG is that many projects stall or stop altogether due to the insecure environment that affects international workers differently to local authorities. The implementation of these suggested options for operational purposes will not compromise the integrity of UN agency mandates or individual donor policy platforms. 
UN Goal and Objectives
For Iraq the UN has identified the scope of people-centred rehabilitation and development necessary to address and realise the overall UN goal of poverty alleviation. Indicators for success across the three key areas - social, economic and governance - vital for sustainable development are:
Broad based, environmentally sustainable, economic growth
Greater empowerment of women and youth
Protection of vulnerable groups including reintegration
Public institutional strengthening, capacity building and upgrading of skills
Greater democratisation, decentralisation, transparency and accountability
Promotion of conflict resolution at national as well as local community level
Building of social capital and a vibrant civil society.
In consideration of this long-term developmental scope the UN has identified three major challenges: (a) promoting the right of access to and making available basic social services, (b) ensuring a broad-based, diversified and environmentally sustainable economic growth, and (c) strengthening institutional and governance capacities and human security within the country. The overall UN Goal for 2005 - 2007 is to:
Contribute significantly to the creation of a secure enabling environment conducive to the fulfilment of the rights of Iraqi people to survival, development and equal participation through achieving the following objectives:
Objective 1:
Improve the quality of and enhanced access to basic social services including food, as well as effective and coordinated humanitarian emergency preparedness and response
Objective 2:
Rehabilitate and develop the country’s social, economic, financial, physical and institutional infrastructure to ensure sustainable livelihoods and durable solutions to displaced populations in the country
Objective 3:
Promote better governance, peace-building, and protection of human rights
This overall goal requires a strategy of continuing to provide humanitarian aid in response to emergencies as well as assistance that supports potential future development.  In effect, the UN will move on from ‘saving lives’ to ‘saving livelihoods’, and the UN’s pro-poor growth strategies as well as adopting the MDGs as the framework against which to measure progress, were explicitly endorsed by international donors at the IRFFI Donors meeting in Tokyo on 13-14 October 2004. The focus, apart from cross-cutting themes, will be on improving emergency preparedness and response, community level interventions, institution strengthening and capacity building and support to policy formulation. 
The three objectives inform and guide a strategy for increasing longer-term interventions to reduce the need for relief operations. Relief activities save lives while life-sustaining activities provide the springboard for the success of post-conflict reconstruction and rehabilitation. However, the achievement of this largely depends on how the political situation evolves. 
The objectives also link closely with Iraq’s development strategy as articulated by Iraq at the IRFFI Donors’ Meeting held in Tokyo.  This document outlines the major orientation for the country in the coming year.  The Government will update the NDS periodically to reflect current realities and needs.  However, it is currently the basic guideline for Iraq’s social and economic development.  Therefore, the UNCT should streamline activities and programmes to the key areas identified in the NDS.
Iraq’s current development strategy as articulated by the then Deputy Prime Minister, Barham Saleh, focuses on three pillars of reform: social development, the economy and good governance.  The UN’s objectives reflect these pillars and will be realised through the “cluster approach”, the structure of which may be reviewed in order to address appropriately the three proposed objectives outlined.  In parallel, security, human rights, gender, employment and environment will continue to make up the cross cutting themes, which will be mainstreamed in all UN programming. To make these themes an objective in itself would be contrary to the mainstreaming philosophy.  Hence, the cross-cutting themes will be addressed and be the enabling factors within each objective.
Objective 1:
Improve the quality of and enhanced access to basic social services including food, as well as effective and coordinated humanitarian emergency preparedness and response
Support the Iraqi Government to strengthen emergency preparedness and resolve ongoing and new displacement challenges to avert future emergencies or at least lessen their impact.  At the same time, better assessment of social conditions, planning, monitoring and evaluation of policies and programmes, should lead to a more effective and efficient provision of basic social services and eventually to greater self-reliance. This will contribute to a better understanding in Iraq of the underlying causes of poverty, to its progressive eradication, and to the achievement of the Millennium Development Goals.
Objective 2:
Rehabilitate and develop the country’s social, economic, financial, physical and institutional infrastructure to ensure sustainable livelihoods and durable solutions to displaced populations in the country
Rehabilitating livelihoods that have been destroyed and helping people to develop sustainable livelihoods through a right-based approach are fundamental to reducing poverty. In addition to mobilising financial resources, this requires mobilising human resources (education, health, skills, training); natural resources (food, land, livestock, water); physical resources (equipment, infrastructure, tools); and social and political resources (community, family and other social networks). Improving information about, and access to these resources is fundamental to empowering the poor and reducing poverty.
Objective 3:
Promote better governance, peace-building and protection of human rights
Peace, good governance, rule-of-law and respect for and protection of human rights are inextricably linked. Reduction of poverty is dependent on progress being made in these areas. 
Once stability and security are achieved, good governance is the vehicle by which respect for human rights is concretely spelled out in policies, strategies and programmes. Government, therefore, needs to be more efficient, effective and accountable while focusing of people-centred development that resolves long-standing issues of inequity including protracted population displacement based on previous political, security and socio-economic prerogatives. Only then can the fundamental principles of human rights, such as non-discrimination, equity and equality attested in law empower people, free creative and productive energy and lift the nation out of the vicious cycle of poverty. This should be measured in terms of compliance with relevant UN conventions and charters covering conflict, human rights, and refugees. Ultimately, however, it must be measured in terms of stability and actual improvement in people’s lives.
Success in meeting the above objectives should contribute to alleviating poverty over the longer term.  However, each objective cannot be achieved in isolation from the other. Long-term self-reliance is not possible without rehabilitation in the social sector and strong agricultural and industrial sectors. Economic development and sustainable livelihoods cannot be achieved without having coherent development policies. These policies cannot be implemented without good governance. An integrated approach is needed to address poverty in a strategic and practical manner. Challenges in the areas of: health, water, sanitation, education, agriculture and industry, food security, environment, employment, reintegration and resettlement, rule of law, justice and public administration have to be prioritised. 
Strategic areas identified for system-wide co-ordination are disaster prevention, mitigation and preparedness, community-level participation and interventions, policy support, advocacy and strengthening local and national capacities.
Operational Framework
Planning correctly is one aspect of the UN’s strategic response; making the plan operational so as to be effective and efficient is equally important. In addition to selecting the most appropriate organisational arrangements and oversight, the UNCT has investigated ways and means of harmonising and improving common services. 
To that end, UNAMI will revitalise the common services task force, with the aim of improved delivery effectiveness and cost efficiency. The principles involved are: (a) building on existing shared services, (b) differentiating between programme and organisational support services, (c) building up incrementally, based on demand, (d) having time-bound agreements, and (e) having transparency and accountability throughout.
There is a concerted effort underway to bring into operation a common services approach that would tie in well with there being only a limited number of Minimum Operational Security Standards (MOSS)-compliant locations in Iraq being available to the UN system for the foreseeable future. As a general principle, common services shall be provided by the agency in whose premises other agencies are located. For now it is a matter of focusing on identifying the provision of common services and shared MOSS-compliant facilities in Iraq – not only in Baghdad but in the North and South of the country.
It is expected that most communications will be electronic in nature supported by teleconferencing and videoconferencing, as the opportunity for face-to-face meetings with UN colleagues outside Iraq, are likely to be limited to those occasion when government officials visit Amman. Eventually, once there is an improvement in the security situation and the UN locations are MOSS-compliant, programme-related international personnel should be permitted to make more regular visits to Baghdad and elsewhere in the country. 
The key for coordination mechanisms and programme (delivery) modalities for each cluster is optimizing utilization of UN national staff across many ministries, directorates, and municipalities, fully supported by the UN international cluster teams in neighbouring Amman and also the UN system as a whole. There are a wide range of procurement modalities for contracting goods, expertise and capacity in support or national initiatives and organisations addressing priority needs and areas in place. The involvement of partners is vital including international and national NGOs, national contractors and consultants, national academic and research institutions, and where possible, civil society groups. 
The day-to-day difficulties being experienced by national staff has led to a number of adaptive modalities. These include virtual home offices, internet, teleconferencing, mobile telephony, videoconferencing, CD interactive training packs, and so on. Mobility modalities include utilising private vehicles, public urban transport, intercity buses, military flights and similar. Access is addressed by holding meetings at ministry offices and warehouses, cross-border meetings, offering staff training outside Iraq, amongst others. As and when the security situation improves the UNCT will look to short trips, which can be extended as circumstances permit. 
The range of services offered by the common services unit will include security arrangements; staff logistics; premises, related to enhanced MOSS compliance; transportation; facility management; information services; medical assistance, and IT where appropriate. The need for providing other services will emerge over time, and will be addressed accordingly.

Introduction
In line with the on-going UN reform process, a results-based, strategic Cluster approach was adopted to guide our actions under the special circumstances obtaining in Iraq. The approach enables the UN agencies to avoid overlapping functions, confusion among their complementary missions with respect to Iraq and wastage of effort and resources. The approach lays a foundation for cost effective, unified and efficient programming initiatives. It also provides UN agencies [and other partners such as the World Bank] with a unique platform for joint analysis, planning and prioritization of action within a mutually agreed framework for action. 
The Education Cluster is one of the 11 clusters making up the system.  UN Partners in this cluster are UNICEF, UNESCO, UNHCR, UN-HABITAT, ESCWA, UNOPS, UNIDO, UNIFEM, OHCHR, WFP, WHO, and ILO. The entire group will work with the World Bank and with the Ministries of Education, Higher Education and Culture, Labour and Social Affairs as well as with NGOs, community groups, international education institutions, donor agencies and the private sector.    
The importance of education 
Among the benefits of education to individuals, it is well documented that it is “the ultimate liberator” which empowers them to make personal decisions. At the group level, education is “the ultimate equalizer” which promotes greater equity for the poor, particularly for women and other disadvantaged groups. In nation-building and in the special conditions of Iraq, education is equally critical since literate and educated citizens are the foundation and the rampart of democratic institutions that ultimately help achieve social cohesion.    
Research has strongly evidenced that education has a positive impact on fertility, maternal and child health, nutrition, environment management and income equality. Educating girls and mothers has proven to be critically important. For example, studies show that mothers who have completed primary education were more likely to get their children fully immunized with all antigens.  
Education is also a necessary condition for creating, applying and spreading the new ideas and technologies indispensable to sustained economic growth. A basic education and a secondary education of quality and a sound higher education system will make Iraq benefit from the ICT (Information Communication Technology) revolution, a critical avenue to the global economy. 
The challenge in Education and Culture
The longer-term challenge in Iraq is multiple. In Education, it involves ensuring provision of quality education for all, re-engaging the whole population in the education process, ensuring clear linkages between the education system and the needs of the country, and maximising the capacity of national institutions and officials to underpin and support key interventions. In the specific realm of Culture, the challenge is to restore the repositories of national culture to a fully operational state and to promote greater national and international cooperation in cultural heritage studies, information sharing and research. The UN’s comparative advantage is based on over two decade engagement with and support for educational development in Iraq, backed up by its world-wide commitment to education and culture.  Its effectiveness is enhanced by professional national staff operating from regional offices, and this human infrastructure offers a unique opportunity for decentralized programming.  In addition, highly qualified international staff, drawing on a broad knowledge base, provides technical leadership and support.  The cluster’s close involvement with government and civil society actors has created a close-knit network that permits rapid and efficient implementation of projects and helps ensure sustainable results.  Equally important is the fact that the UN is recognized by Iraqis as a credible voice on behalf of women and children’s rights - and their right to quality education in particular - which helps make the organization an effective advocate. At the same time, the UN’s commitment to preservation, protection and enrichment of the region’s human heritage puts it in a uniquely strong position to mobilise resources and raise awareness on cultural issues.
Context 
Iraq embodies both complex challenges and unique opportunities. Education has traditionally been very highly valued at all levels of Iraqi society – from the family through the community to all levels of government. Before the wars of the last two decades, the Iraqi education system from the pre-primary schooling through university education was well developed. The single most important development is that the Interim and future Transitional Authorities are providing the reconstruction efforts with leadership and guidance. Additionally, it is increasingly focusing on coordination of partner intervention which augurs well for increased local ownership backed up by the existence of dedicated and knowledgeable Iraqi educationists rising to the challenge. These constitute factors that enhance the prospects for a rebirth and modernization of a system that made the nation proud in the 70s.  
On the other hand, the wars seriously degraded both the equipment and the personnel of the system:  school buildings, textbooks production and distribution facilities, etc. were destroyed or extensively damaged. In addition, the conflicts and the sanctions of the 90s took their toll on the health status of many children and their caregivers and as a consequence had very negative effects on enrolment and attendance. The system is now faced with some severe problems. At the primary level, it is plagued by large enrolment and gender gaps between governorates and between urban and rural areas; increasing repetition rate; a low transition rate from primary to secondary – only 52% of children completing primary school are enrolled in secondary school. 
The situation at the secondary level is even more alarming. The Gross Enrolment Rate stands at only 42% and there is a 12% gender gap (in the Net Enrolment Rate) and a 31% discrepancy between rates in urban and rural areas, plus an average class repetition rate of 9% (MOE-UNICEF, 2005). Overall, quality remains a preoccupying issue at both primary and secondary levels of the system. Notwithstanding these drawbacks, Iraq as a whole is still characterized, at the primary education level, by an encouraging GER of 98% and an NER of 86 %  - - down from a GER of  109% and an NER of 93 % recorded in the 2000 EFA Assessment (UNESCO, 2000). 
Much is expected of Higher Education and training to help cope with shifting imperatives in Iraq; however, the impact of the last two wars on one hand and the economic and technological change on the other pose new daunting challenges to the sub-sector. If not dealt with in time and in an adequate manner, these challenges can unravel, in future, a whole set of social and political problems with inevitable consequences. The main challenges facing higher education in Iraq are in the key areas of (a) Relevance, (b) Quality and (c) Internationalization. Responses to these challenges necessarily imply shaping of national and institutional policies concerning the missions and functions of higher education in promoting sustainable human development as well as the principles of civil society, and reducing poverty. Hence, a new vision of higher education is needed which combines the demands for universality of higher learning with imperatives for greater relevance, in order to respond to the expectations of the Iraqi society. This vision will stress the principles of academic freedom and institutional autonomy while at the same time emphasise the need for accountability to the society.
When it comes to Culture Heritage, Iraq has a tremendous treasure to protect and preserve. This treasure has been valued by the Iraqi Government, but the events of the last decade have prevented official institutions to act properly in the fields of protection and conservation. Being a country harbouring one of the oldest civilizations with archaeological and historical sites scattered all over its surface, UNESCO has put priority on Culture Heritage conservation, with special focus on the protection of archaeological sites and museums in the aftermath of the war. This is of the utmost importance, in view of the damage caused, and the on-going pillaging of some of these sites.  Training and equipment has been provided and will be needed in the following areas: protection and conservation; empowering the Iraqi national system, institutions and facilities, especially looking at job creation; rehabilitation of cultural premises and research institutions; documentation of cultural property through the development of inventories and database; and rebuilt national identity through heritage conservation.
Furthermore it is important to pay attention at the conservation and revitalization of intangible cultural heritage. Therefore institutions and centres promoting traditional culture such as music, dance and poetry are being supported in an effort to preserve the existing diversity in Iraqi culture and build on the way to understanding and tolerance.

Preface
This review has been carried out without substantial consultation with the MoA or the MoWR, our main counterpart ministries owing to the time constraint. Some consultation took place when representatives of these Ministries, as well as of the Ministry of Planning came to Amman to participate in the Workshop on the FAO Socio-economic Surveys of Rural Areas in early December. The review also incorporated the expressed priority list provided by the Minister of Agriculture as well as the NDS document.
Objectives of Cluster 5
The main objectives of programmes are to promote sustainable and environmentally sound development and to ensure effective management of natural resources, which benefits people, communities and their environment. Cluster 5 takes the concerted approach by participating agencies in order to focus on immediate needs such as the restoration of critical agricultural infrastructure and service as well as supports to the long-term human needs. It also addresses policy and institutional reform issues in water resources and environmental management through capacity building and human resources development.
Agriculture - Background
The NDS clearly identifies the critical situation of the agricultural sector; specifically The NDS clearly identifies the critical situation of the agricultural sector, specifically the reduction in productivity leading to the drastic decline in per capita agricultural production.   While the connection is made between the previous policy of keeping food prices artificially low and the decline in agricultural production, there is scope for further exploration of the implications of a reversal of this policy.  Revitalization of the agricultural sector needs to be closely aligned with reform of the Public Distribution System (PDS).  The transition from the current situation of subsidized agricultural inputs and low output prices to a relatively free market will have to be gradual in order to avoid a breakdown in supply.  Small farmers will require assistance to operate effectively under the new policy environment.
Overall there is a requirement to develop further the strategy for the agricultural and rural sector in order to provide a coherent context within which to prioritize actions.  At the same time, there is an urgent need to initiate some activities on the ground in order to assist poor farmers.  It is clear that the actions prioritized so far lack the full strategic framework and it would be desirable to work on this a priori.  However, the majority of actions already proposed are likely to remain important as the needs are so great.
Prioritized Actions
The prioritized actions indicated in the NDS document do not always match the project proposals indicated as priorities by MoA at the Tokyo Donors Conference in October.
One area where there is a clear match is with respect to provision of improved seeds. High quality seed of improved varieties is one of the most critical inputs for a sustainable agricultural production system and the seed industry in Iraq is presently hardly functioning and unable to meet farmers’ needs for improved cultivars as the certified seed production system has broken down. In this context, FAO, in consultation with Iraqi specialists, has prepared a US$ 5.1 million Rehabilitation and Development of the National Seed Industry in Iraq project.  The main objective is to improve the performance of the national seed industry through the formulation of a national seed policy supplemented by review and consolidation of existing seed legislation, rehabilitation of damaged infrastructure and improvement of technical capacity through training.  The outcome will be provision of a sound foundation to a revitalized, sustainable seed industry.  As a result of project activities, breeder seed for main cereal crops will be produced locally and variety maintenance techniques and procedures for the target crops will be developed.  This project is ready for Cluster Peer Review and submission to the UNDG Trust Fund Steering Committee.
The NDS document makes several references to the need for improved veterinary services and FAO is already addressing this requirement through its ongoing Restoration of Veterinary Services project.  The focus of this project is on provision of veterinary supplies and extensive training.
Fish are only mentioned in the context of protecting animal assets in the NDS, but the project for Restoration and Modernization of Fish Production in Iraq is given priority in the proposals presented at Tokyo.  A US$6.5 million project has been prepared by FAO in close consultation with Iraqi specialists.  The most promising avenue for development in the short term lies in restoring and expanding the fish farming sub-sector. In the required context of a two-year programme, priority has therefore been assigned to rehabilitation of the main Government fish hatchery and resuscitation of aquaculture production by small fishermen.   This is considered the most promising means to rapidly increase domestic production of fish thereby increasing domestic availability of urgently needed protein to the Iraqi people.  The project will also restore lost employment opportunities and add new ones. Increased production will reduce fish imports, currently at about 27 000 t per year. A revitalized and expanded industry will increase upstream and downstream supporting industries, such as the production of seed, feed and fertilizer and the manufacture of specialized equipment (water aerators and automatic feeders, etc.) providing additional employment and contributing to GNP. This project is ready for Cluster Managers approval and submission to the UNDG Trust Fund Steering Committee.
Capacity building is mentioned directly in the NDS and also implied in proposals such as the one to expand agricultural counselling services.  There is also a project proposal presented at the Tokyo Conference for Rebuilding the Capacity of Iraqi Scientists and Facilities to support Improvements in Agricultural Production.  Earlier in the year FAO did some preliminary work on a proposal for strengthening the agricultural extension services, and this could be substantiated and finalized if required.  All ongoing and already prepared projects have significant components of capacity building. 
There is an FAO Regional Project for IPM (Integrated Pest Management).  While Iraq is not a mainstream participant in this project, it has the status of Observer.  Although a US$ 25 million proposal was put forward at Tokyo, in the current context, a pilot approach with a specific crop is considered the best way to initiate activities in Iraq.  It may be possible to include an IPM component in the proposed Date Palm Sector Rehabilitation Programme being developed under Cluster 5 with the assistance of both FAO and UNIDO.  
While animal and plant quarantine services have been grouped together in both the NDS and the Tokyo project proposals, the approach required is different.  Animal quarantine is an activity requiring inspection and holding grounds at border points and land boundaries are particularly difficult to patrol in the current situation.  It is suggested that this proposal be postponed.  On the other hand, plant inspection may be handled in the context of food safety.  A project addressing food safety issues are currently being developed jointly by WHO, FAO and UNIDO under Cluster 2.
An important area for the Cluster to consider in the light of indicated Government priorities is that of environmental protection and land management.  Areas of concern identified in the NDS and the Tokyo proposals include desertification control, maintenance of natural grazing lands and forestry rehabilitation.
Once an overall strategy is developed, it is likely that the critical contribution of complementary services, such as credit and rural infrastructure will be acknowledged and project proposals developed accordingly.
Water Resources - Background
The NDS clearly identifies the requirement for a water resource master plan. UNESCO has started work on this and FAO is keen to contribute. The formulation of the comprehensive water resources master plan requires to all water consuming sectors and related UN agencies to be involved under Cluster approach. The formulation process will take a phased approach and long time to finalize and Cluster 5 is set to address the early phase. In particular, the scope for integrating the establishment of a Hydrological and Agro-meteorological Network should be investigated to conduct water resources assessment as FAO prepared a proposal for this in 2003, which could be reworked to fit into the plan.  The World Bank is also planning its Country Water Resources Assistance Strategy (CWRAS) and the latest news is that Minister of MoWR has expressed a preference for a formal workshop on this after the elections.  
There is a chance here for the UN to move ahead in support the Government in further definition of its own strategy and thereby help to “set the agenda” for World Bank assistance. It would be particularly important to have some initial/informal brainstorming on the proposal for the master plan with MoWR officials attending the survey workshop.
Priorities
It is encouraging that the NDS sets high priority on the need to work with neighbours on agreements for sharing the waters of the Tigris/Euphrates river basin since 75% of available water resources in Iraq originate outside of the country. Even though there will need to be strong political will to reach the goal, UNESCO will work on shared water resources based on experiences in this field. 
Technical and institutional capacity building and human resources development of MoWR are main objectives of on-going UNESCO’s Capacity Building in Water Institutions project. This project is expected to lead to the formulation of the updated National Water Master Plan.
Capacity building for Hydrological study and research has already started within the framework of the Cluster’s on-going projects, and the full-fledged studies as the fundamental for formulating water policy and strategy could be included in the Master Plan project whereby UNESCO is taking the lead and FAO and UNEP will also make a contribution. Furthermore, under the ongoing irrigation projects, a detailed proposal for training is being developed by the Cluster.  A consultant has already been hired and the proposal already sent for review by MoWR and MOA. This training would be both for technicians and farmers with emphasis on more efficient use of water. 
FAO is already working with MoWR on three irrigation/drainage projects and is thus fully compliant with the priority requirements to renovate existing projects and proceed with implementation of committed ones.  Irrigation projects with their very specific locations present a special challenge in the current security situation.
With respect to maintenance, more attention should be given to financial requirements and the need for local ownership. Until beneficiaries of irrigation schemes contribute to the maintenance, there will be little incentive on the part of users to minimize such costs by taking greater care of facilities and requirements will continue to exceed the availability of resources.
FAO is already working with MoWR on the renovation of pumping stations. Successful accomplishment of the initial project will pave the way for additional support.
Numerous activities supported by a range of donors are planned for the Marshlands. UNEP is taking the lead in this activity. However, the FAO considers it has expertise in the areas of Marshland Hydraulics and the Ecosystem Management and would like to participate in the Task Management Groups set up in these areas.
Tokyo Projects
The projects put forward by MoWR at Tokyo are mostly large-scale and beyond the resources of the UNDG Trust Fund.  While FAO would be happy to participate in certain projects, particularly where the emphasis is on improving livelihoods of small farmers, current priority in the sector is being given to implementation of ongoing projects and the water resources master plan.
Agro-industry - Background
The NDS makes no reference to agro-industry related prioritized actions.  However, this does not obviate the need for action in this sector.  The government has begun to develop agricultural policies and institutional reform that will provide the basis for food security in the medium-term, including capacity building of the private sector and phasing out subsidies. The current cost of the public food distribution system costs $4.6 billion.  In order for Iraq to minimize the impact of trade deficits of importing all its food basket contents, it must start to gradually and methodically revitalize many of its state owned enterprises and private sector firms in the food production sector.  This is on condition that their rehabilitation or establishment meets the strategic objectives of Iraq. 
Prioritized action
Of particular importance is fertilizer production as mentioned in the NDS.  In addition to this, cereals processing and packaging, vegetable canning and freezing, other locally grown and marketable products like dates and pulses, as well as insecticide manufacturing.  
In order to achieve a measure of success in this sector, UNIDO has begun implementation of two key projects. One is the dairy sector pilot rehabilitation project and the other is the cottage industry project with FAO.  The former seeks to eventually build up key upstream activities with FAO (like cow and buffalo breeding, milk collection depot networks) and downstream such as other value added dairy products like cheese and yoghurt. The cottage industry project seeks to build up cottage food and non-food sector businesses through capacity building. UNIDO is also working together with the FAO in the development of the date palm sector. 
Environment - Background
The National Development Strategy identifies “environment protection” as a sector under the Sector Development Programmes. The NDS targets to a) explore options to introduce emissions standards and phase out old vehicles, b) to conduct a comprehensive environmental assessment of water, air and soil conditions in Iraq, identifying sources and extent of contamination, and needed remedies, c) to assess the current legal and regulatory framework for the environment and the requirements for improving environment protection in Iraq, d) promote the financial, human and technical capacity of the Ministry of Environment, to facilitate building an effective environment surveillance and control system, and e) to protect the natural balance through expanding forests and natural conservation projects and maintaining environmental systems.
Earlier studies by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) have identified the following chronic environmental problems:

Destruction of oil infrastructure

However, before Iraq’s environmental problems can be properly addressed, the country’s institutions for environmental governance at national, governorate and local level, including legal frameworks and policies, must be rebuilt and strengthened. 
Prioritized Actions
The United Nations Environment Programme is actively responding to these needs. Further to the Desk Study on the Environment in Iraq (March 2003) and the UNEP Progress Report on Environment in Iraq (October 2003), UNEP has established presence in the United Nations Country Team for Iraq. The Iraq Trust Fund approved two projects on “capacity and institution building for environmental governance” (US$ 4.7 million) and “rehabilitation of the Iraqi Marshlands through introduction of environmentally sound technologies” (US$ 11 million) both earmarked by the Government of Japan. The World Bank will invest US$ 25 million in the “Iraq Emergency Environmental Management Project”, which targets to strengthen Iraq’s environmental management capacity and improve environmental conditions in selected areas”.
Implementation of UNEP’s capacity building project has started in September 2004 and will continue throughout 200It strengthens the Iraqi environmental management capacity to deal with environmental policy and law making, contamination and exposure of the population to health risks. It targets primarily the newly established Ministry of Environment with support in the areas of environmental law development (including support to establishing a right to a clean environment in the new Constitution), environmental site assessment, environmental impact assessment, environmental governance, environmental monitoring, etc. This support promotes Iraq’s ratification and accession to the Multilateral Environment Agreements, which in the longer term will lead to financial and capacity building support for environmental remediation projects.

Developing an environmental impact assessment process, and applying environmental safeguard policies, is essential for environmentally sound reconstruction of Iraq. Once the security situation improves and economic activity picks up, Iraq has the potential to be a destination of rapid investment in industrial revitalisation. Mine Action
Decades of wars and internal conflicts have left Iraq with a serious Explosive Remnants of War (ERW - landmines, unexploded ordnance and explosive ordnances), and in some parts a depleted uranium (DU) munitions contamination problem. 
The United Nations Development Group (UNDG)/World Bank Joint Needs Assessment in Iraq conducted in 2003, and the mine action strategy of the National Mine Action Authority (NMAA), have concluded that in many areas, the most serious threat faced by Iraqi civilians is that resulting from explosive ordnance (EO) pre-positioned in preparation for the war of early 2003 and shifted during post-war looting. Additionally, unexploded ordnance (UXO) are scattered throughout many of the major cities, villages, and military positions affected by recent and earlier conflicts, including cluster and depleted uranium munitions. 
The ERW contamination throughout Iraq poses a serious threat to the safety of the civilian population by denying access to valuable resources including agricultural land, grazing land, roads, water sources and residential areas. In many parts of the country the ERW contamination hinders the safe return of internally displaced persons and refugees. Moreover, the ERW contamination is considered one of the major challenges in the implementation of relief, rehabilitation, reconstruction, and development projects and programmes in the country.
The immediate challenge is to reduce the number of casualties caused by ERW contamination by educating Iraqi civilian population to live safely in an unsafe environment and clearing high priority affected areas. The longer-term challenge is to respect the right of the Iraqi people to live free from the threat of ERW and to receive assistance to become ERW impact free, in accordance with the Ottawa Treaty on Landmines, and other relevant international conventions. The National Mine Action Authority (NMAA), as part of the Ministry of Planning and Development Cooperation, took full responsibility for addressing the serious ERW situation facing Iraq. The NMAA needs to focus on the following pillars of mine action in support of the National Development Strategy (NDS):
Clearance of mines, unexploded ordnance (UXO), and explosive ordnance (EO), include dealing with depleted uranium (DU) munitions.
Mine Risk Education.
Mine and UXO Victims Assistance.
Advocacy.
To enable the NMAA to perform this vital task, institutional and capacity building support is of the highest importance.
