Introduction
The turbulent history of Iraq over the past 30 years, to a large extent, has had a devastating impact on the social, political, physical and human capital of the country. The social and political capital comprises the country’s laws, institutions, culture and traditions that underpin the social fabric, enabling the overall governance of the country.  Such institutions include political, legal, judicial, and military entities as well as police, civil society, the media and other public and private entities that are the ultimate source of authority and trust.  To restore the torn Iraqi social fabric and reduce    violence and conflict, rebuilding and investing in the political and social capital is the major task facing Iraqis and the international community today. 

The journey to socio-economic and political stability may take several generations, but Iraq has the necessary human, cultural and economic foundation to forge ahead once the violence subsides. Most Iraqis are eager to re-build their lives, communities and institutions - after years of isolation - and want to take their place within the wider global community.
The UN has the daunting task of providing support to Iraqi institutions: government, civil society, media and others to help Iraqis re-build their war-torn country.
 
The challenge in Governance & Civil Society
The process of nation building involves a series of transformations: political, structural, social and economic. Iraqi policy makers and the international community face the challenge of creating a national restructuring framework, undertaking substantial policy reforms that will allow Iraqis to rebuild their institutions and achieve the necessary transformations. The guiding principles of the UN efforts towards the reconstruction of Iraq are based on the following:
That reforms and interventions are Iraqi-led, involving government, civil society, private sector, media from all social and economic strata and that priorities are identified by Iraqis themselves;
That national reconstruction efforts are channelled towards alleviating poverty incorporating the Millennium Development Goals; and 
That the National Development Strategy (NDS) is updated with emphasis on social and human development policies and reforms, in order to reduce poverty and regional disparity and to further reduce the risk of conflict and violence. 
Issues, Priorities of Reforms
Public sector reform and strengthening institutional/administrative infrastructure
In the past decade, most of the state apparatus was neglected. Soon after the fall of the previous regime, many government institutions and ministries were looted, destroyed and public goods and archival materials destroyed. Iraqi public institutions face several obstacles: competent staff have either been fired, fled the country or in worst cases killed; records and infrastructure have been destroyed. Thus, policies, regulatory affairs, public service programmes must be developed from scratch. 
Well-functioning public institutions are fundamental to sustainable development and a pre-condition in improving the livelihood of the population. Working with Iraqi counterparts, UN efforts will be targeted towards strengthening and restructuring public institutions. As well UN will provide support to the Government’s wider public service reform agenda, identified in the NDS. Needs assessment to establish a modern Iraqi School for Management Development and Public Service Commission will be conducted.
The Ministries of Human Rights, Justice, Civil Society and others require immediate support to build institutional, organizational and human resources capacity in most areas, including: policy planning, general management, programme delivery, citizen’s participation, among others.
Strengthening local governments and institutions
For decades, Iraq remained a centrally-governed state with very little devolution of authority to the local administration. Most national and international experts and research indicate that Iraqi local administration and municipalities are unable to provide some of the basic services to the population. Local administrations require rebuilding and do not have the institutional and human resource capacity necessary to perform their tasks. Working with Iraqi research team, UN will conduct an assessment on local government issues and initiate programmes to strengthen the municipalities’ local governance capabilities and train staff in participatory governance and service delivery, with pilots in two municipalities. Pilots, with private/public partnerships in service delivery opportunities will be explored.

NGOs, CSOs, human rights, women’s equality
The most basic tenets of democratic practice require broad acceptance by the state and civil society. Whether in Iraq or elsewhere, this is a complex, gradual and delicate process. In the past twelve months, the non-government and civil society sector, in Iraq has multiplied. Most of these nascent human rights organizations are not yet sufficiently well established to operate effectively, nor are they in a position to influence public debate. Training and capacity building efforts by UN and its agencies and INGOs will continue to focus on training human rights organizations, CSOs and women’s groups on the basic principles of human rights and gender equality.
Women’s groups appear to be active at the community level. These groups provide basic community services such as health, education and family support. UN agencies are well placed to continue support of these institutions. However, the exodus of INGOs due to security reasons and the incapacity of local NGOs to operate at the community level due to similar reasons, jeopardize these institutions that are the pillars of grass roots democratic movement.
Reintegration of all uprooted people (IDPs, refugees). Integration of IDPs, refugees is a major challenge for the Government. The Ministry of Displacement and Migration has the mandate to address some of the social and integration issues. However, adequate priority has yet to be given to the right to return, resettlement and reintegration of these groups. Many UN organizations are working with the Iraqi Government and NGOs working with refugees and IDPs, to provide support and address the larger protection issues. The support of the international community is needed to address the fair resettlement issue of IDPs and refugees. 
Freedom of expression and the development of non-partisan and independent media
The importance of a free press for encouraging democratic tendencies and respect for human and civil rights is well recognized. Conversely, the dissemination of distorted or biased information can fuel tensions in unstable environments. In the case of Iraq, the media has seen extreme situations in a short period. Where the media was controlled and suppressed under the previous regime, the media has undergone a major transformation. Community, local press as well as radio and television stations have been established with varied capacity and professionalism.  UN has developed a full, multiyear programme to support Iraqi media development programmes that include capacity building, institutional strengthening and web-based news exchange initiatives. 
Key comparative advantage
The key comparative advantage of the UN is a high degree of legitimacy as a neutral actor. A collaborative work environment has already been established between key Iraqi stakeholders and UN Agencies, the latter familiar with the challenges facing Iraqis. Support to the Electoral Process
Electoral mandate and concept of operations
SCR 1546 mandated UNAMI to facilitate the task of the IECI. This mandate was made more concrete by a request from the IECI Commissioners for the UN to provide technical assistance and to coordinate international electoral support.
The operational concept envisaged a number of technical experts from the UN, together with technical experts from other organizations and donors, working with the IECI under the coordination of the head of the UNAMI elections section. These experts, based in the Commission's headquarters in Baghdad, would assist and advise both the Board of Commissioners and the Electoral Administration in their tasks.
In addition to the coordination of the technical assistance, the UNAMI elections section would also coordinate other forms of electoral assistance being provided, as well as coordinating and mobilizing resources. Such coordination under the UN was obviously necessary for the prevention of duplication, and in order to ensure proper use of resources.
Coordination of international electoral support
The international Electoral Assistance Team comprised both UN experts and experts from other organizations, and at its height numbered around 42 people, of whom more than half were from the UN. All staff worked under the coordination of the Chief Electoral Adviser of UNAMI, and this resulted in a successful integrated team.
In addition, the UN mobilized donor resources, largely through cluster 11 which used over $108 million to fund activities, while bilateral earmarked funds totaled over $132 million. UNDP Iraq provided additional funding, as did IFES, in consultation with the UN. 
An international contact group was established in Baghdad, with the aim of sharing information and coordinating donor activity. This group met on a weekly basis throughout the electoral process, facilitating close contacts and transparency of information.
Provision of technical assistance
Following SCR 1546, and requests from the Independent Electoral Commission of Iraq, the UN agreed to provide technical assistance and to coordinate all international electoral assistance, including both technical assistance and donor support. The Electoral Assistance Team providing technical assistance to the IECI comprised UN electoral experts together with experts from the EU, from the UK, and from IFES, and worked under the coordination of the UN international commissioner, in his role as Chief Electoral Officer for UNAMI. This coordination ensured both that there was no overlap in technical assistance provided by the various bodies and also that all policies and decisions met international standards. Additionally, a support team in Amman collaborated on issues that could be completed outside Iraq. 
The UN areas of activity in 2005 include the following:
Continuation of support to IECI by providing technical assistance with the emphasis on capacity building.  The UN electoral support team had to concentrate for the past 8 months on trainings on operational activities leading to the January 30th election date.  Due to the very tight timeframe, there has been no long-term training, which would assist the IECI in its capacity building of their staff.  The trainings will include operational administration, finance, human resources, logistics, public outreach and civic education.  
The UN has been the leading agency and the main coordinating body for international technical assistance provided to the IECI.  This role will continue in support to the IECI’s preparation for the referendum scheduled for October 2005 followed by the General Elections in the country based on the constitution. 
The United Nations is likely to be playing an important role in support to the discussions that will be taking place within the National Assembly on the electoral design.    
The support provided by the Electoral Assistance Team, under the coordination of the UN, was very effective, and it is clear that the elections would not have been successful without this support. However, it was also important that the support was ‘behind the scenes’, with the responsibility for the elections being seen to rest with the IECI, and all elements of the process seen to be led by Iraqis; this increased the effectiveness of the support. Indeed, the success of the elections is essentially because the Iraqis rose to the occasion: not only Electoral Administration staff, but also polling staff, voters, monitors and observers defied threats and intimidation in order to take part in the elections.
However, it should be noted that the support provided by the Electoral Assistance Team was at times difficult to implement, and it lacked timeliness, particularly in the initial stages. UN security restrictions also caused some difficulties in effecting the work.
Nonetheless, as a result of the work over the last 8 months, and the support of the EAT, the IECI is now seen as a credible, capable and independent elections management body. The success of the 30 January 30 elections, together with the impartiality of the Board throughout the complaints process, has enhanced this credibility.
Recommendations
Although the IECI has developed considerably over the past months, there is a considerable need for consolidating its status and its capacities. There are many challenges ahead, and, in order to meet them, it is important that UN support to the IECI is continued, and possibly expanded. The support will need to be two-pronged: capacity building for the IECI must run alongside the operational support for the referendum and the general elections. At the same time, although necessarily separate, there will be a role for the UN in supporting the discussion on electoral modalities within the constitutional debate.
The UN’s coordination of assistance was also crucial to the process; it enabled the transparent sharing of information, good coordination of donor activity, and cohesion in the technical assistance. It is vital that this coordination role is continued and that the institutional space won by the UN on the electoral sphere be maintained.
Support to the IECI
The support required by the IECI involves both capacity building and operational support. The focus during this election was on setting up the institution at the same time as ensuring that the elections could take place before the end of January 2005, and the capacity building was largely limited to on-the-job training. There now needs to be a concerted approach to capacity building training; this needs to be instituted urgently, since the focus will very shortly shift to the operational assistance necessary for the elections later in the year. I will be important to revise the institutional design, the role of the various electoral officers (including commissioners and electoral administrators), mainstreaming of decision-making and administrative procedures. Emphasis should also be placed in strengthening the capacity of the field offices.
Operational support for the referendum, due in mid-October, and for the general elections, due in mid-December, must clearly run in parallel; given the timeframe, a sequential approach is not recommended - concentration on the referendum alone would force a significant delay in the general elections. Substantial support will be required, as the running of two completely separate elections at different dates but in parallel will be vastly more challenging even than the preparation for the 30 January elections. In addition, given the requirements for approval of the constitution on a governorate level, issues of districting may need to be considered.
Support to the constitutional debate
The definition of electoral modalities will be a key and sensitive element of the constitutional debate. Technical support to definition of electoral modalities will be required, and the UN should be involved in this from an early stage. Given the timeframe, it will be important for different options to be presented to the constitutional committees, along with linked legal frameworks. This will obviously need to be coordinated with the IECI, since the constitutional decisions will affect the operational requirements particularly for the December elections. At the same time, however, it is important for the IECI to be isolated from the major political discussions regarding the electoral constitutional provisions, in order to protect its perceived independence, neutrality and impartiality.

The common goal, objectives and strategic areas, which have been identified in this document, will form the basis of a strengthened partnership between the UN agencies, clusters and programmes. Each UN Cluster will use this UN Assistance Framework as a tool to aid design and implementation of its country programmes and to look for linkages between the various organisational mandates and sector imperatives across clusters. Co-ordination will also be strengthened in the field of security, communication and logistics. To achieve better inter-agency/inter-cluster co-operation – UN system follow-up and monitoring mechanisms will be strengthened.
Clear and realistic objectives, strategies and outcomes, in the context of funding from both the Iraq Trust Fund and regular agency programming resources, should be regularly iterated to the IIG, Donors, NGO’s and other stakeholders. All partners should routinely share information through formal mechanisms in order to ensure comprehensive ownership of the process and to encourage better co-ordination of the wider developmental effort, including introduction of complementary programming in the future.
Achieving the UN objectives, however, will largely depend on the evolving political situation and the availability of funds, which is difficult to predict especially for the agencies without regular programming resources. Taking into consideration the ongoing conflicts, the insecurity and the limited access to Iraq as a whole in light of UN international staffing ceilings, a cautious approach needs to be adopted. The preceding programme option framework has been designed with the assumption that cluster programming will include both regular programming resources as well as Iraq Trust Fund resources. 
Monitoring and evaluation mechanisms will regularly review progress with Government and other relevant partners. These mechanisms will also review setbacks, and recommend any necessary adjustments or updates to this framework – which should be an organic document that is flexible to change and therefore hopefully will always reflect the current needs of Iraqis. 
Work plans should reflect the ongoing activities related to each objective for each cluster as well as identifying areas for collaborative or parallel programming and opportunities for joint programming across clusters.  Furthermore, all clusters should ensure their programmes and projects meet higher level criteria such as addressing the greatest need, reaching the greatest numbers of beneficiaries particularly the most vulnerable, equity in the geographic distribution of programmes and projects, maximising the opportunity for income generation, ensuring sustainability, meeting security concerns within a rights based framework.
The general principles for prioritising programmes within a cluster are:
must follow the UN’s mandate, and address the Millennium Development Goals, directly or indirectly through a human rights-based approach
must be explicitly based on Iraq’s national priorities and needs, as noted in the public domain, to relevant needs assessments and the National Development Strategy
must promote and ensure national ownership and sustainability
the UN response must be designed appropriate to beneficiary needs, be effective, coherent, context-sensitive, cost-efficient, avoid duplication with other interventions and use strategic entry points that facilitate longer term improvement and sustainability
operational arrangements must explicitly address the questions of limited international access, and coordinated cross-border support and communications
The key requirement is for clusters and agencies is to utilise their regular programming and bilateral funding initially before seeking further support from the Iraq Trust Fund and within the Trust Fund using earmarked funds before applying for un-earmarked funds. 
It is clear that the allocation of funding is not a straightforward exercise. What is required is a best effort, within the context of evolving priorities, to ensure funding flows quickly to those programmes and projects that remove suffering from the most people, generate employment, take into consideration the need for regional equity without compromising effective delivery overall, and can be implemented in 2005 into 2006.

COORDINATION MECHANISMS AND PROGRAMME MODALITIES:

Task Manager: Maman Sidikou (UNICEF)

Deputy Task Manager: Qutub Khan (UNESCO)

UNICEF Staff:
In Iraq- UNICEF has 8 well qualified education staff between the Baghdad, Erbil and Basra offices. Three additional staff members are expected to be recruited as soon as the security conditions on ground improve. In addition, UNICEF has full fledged operations, supply / logistics & finance support units in the Baghdad, Erbil and Basra offices which support education as well as other sectoral programmes.
Outside Iraq- With the recent evacuation of international staff of UNICEF to Amman, the senior international education officer [head of section], and 2 project officers education are now located in Amman temporarily. As in the case of Iraq, the senior and highly experienced international Operations, Supply / logistics and finance officers and staff are now temporarily located in Amman and support the programme implementation there from.
Outsourcing of Services and partner agreements with MOE and NGOs- Given the realities on ground, UNICEF has contracted a number of agencies, which are providing services of 24 experts, senior and professional education monitors [one monitor per DOE in central / south Iraq and Kurdistan] and 10 civil engineers on an ongoing basis. In addition, UNICEF has obtained the services of at least 30 other professionals / semi professionals through similar contractual arrangements though on a short-term basis for specific activities. UNICEF is also increasingly entering in to agreements with NGO partners to expand outreach of its programmes. Most importantly, UNICEF has entered into specific project agreements with the Ministry of education at the National / Directorate levels for implementation and management of the key activities in the education sector (Example: Distribution of education kits and textbooks, conduct of school survey, planning for start up of teacher training activities etc.)

UNESCO Staff:
In Iraq- UNESCO has 11 well qualified education national staff in Baghdad of whom 9 are working for the textbooks project. In addition, 3 national education staff members are currently posted in Erbil.
Outside Iraq- With the relocation of the international staff in Amman, UNESCO, for the time being, is operating out of Amman UNESCO Office. 1 International Education Planner is coordinating activities assisted by 1 clerical assistant and a driver.  In addition, 4 staff members are coordinating the school textbooks project. 
Outsourcing of Services and partner agreements with MOE and NGOs- Given the realities on ground, UNESCO has established strong working relationships with MOE / DOE and MOHE as well as with other UN Agencies to carry out various activities. It is planned that the Universities and other institutions will be identified in the future to support programme implementation in specific areas. 


UN-HABITAT Staff
•	In Iraq – UN-HABITAT has 7 well-qualified national staff and 23 national consultants who have accumulated substantial experience in the construction and rehabilitation of schools and technical institutes in Iraq.
•	Outside Iraq – With the relocation of international staff, UN-HABITAT, for the time being, is operating out of offices in Amman and Kuwait with 4 international and 3 national staff in each of these locations. The Kuwait Office has recently been made the focal point for the management of projects in Iraq.
•   Outsourcing of Services and Partner Agreements with MOE and NGOs – Given its heavy involvement in the rehabilitation of educational infrastructure and its commitment to promoting the development of the small enterprise sector and stimulating employment, UN-HABITAT is selecting contractors and suppliers from a roster of over 450 small contractors and local suppliers throughout the central and southern regions of Iraq. Action is also being taken to establish partnership arrangements with private Engineering companies to further augment the capacity to deliver rehabilitation works on the ground. UN-HABITAT has also established strong working relationships both with the central Ministries of Education and Higher Education in Baghdad and with the Educational Directorates at the Governorate level. 

Inter-  Agency Coordination: 
UNICEF has the nodal responsibility for the development and implementation of Early Childhood and, Primary & Intermediate levels of education while UNESCO has the nodal responsibility for the development and implementation of the Secondary, Tertiary and Vocational / technical levels of education. Both UNICEF and UNESCO will actively harmonize their activities to ensure continuity between various levels of education. 

All activities will be implemented by UNICEF / UNESCO in close collaboration with MOE / DOE, MOHE, other local authorities as well as international / national partners specially the NGOs, civil society, private sector and Donors.

UNICEF and UNESCO will actively collaborate with the following UN agencies to benefit from their technical expertise, area of specialization and comparative advantage and, so as to obtain the best possible synergy of actions on ground:
UN-HABITAT: For establishment of standards and designs in the area of rehabilitation of schools and educational buildings and rehabilitation of some schools / sites  
UNIDO: For technical expertise and support to the design and production of local school furniture. 
WHO: For development and implementation of a comprehensive school health education / promotion programme on a pilot basis and, to integrate school health, personal hygiene, environmental sanitation, nutrition messages / activities in the new education policy and curriculum as the same is revised.  In addition WHO will also provide technical assistance in Health profession education and related areas such as physical rehabilitation / renovation of health education institutions, provision of teaching / learning materials, review and reform curriculum.
UNFPA: For development and integration of reproductive health care education and activities in the new education policy and curriculum, as the same is revised. 
WFP: For initiation of a pilot project on school feeding based on strategies and project design agreed to between various national and international partners. Also see cluster number 6 on food security.
UNIFEM: On gender related issues in education particularly at the time of revision of the education policy and the curriculum.
ESCWA: On providing technical and institutional support for building the capacities of counterparts at the secondary and tertiary education levels, in particular, in the areas of Information and communication technology.
OHCHR: Technical inputs for review of the curriculum and the education policy framework within a human rights perspective.

Linkages with Iraqi Authorities and other actors:
An Education Sector Coordination Forum has already been established inside Iraq under MOE with facilitation from UNICEF. This forum regularly meets on a fortnightly basis and brings together all education partners including the MOE / DOEs, NGOs, Donors and UN agencies for information sharing, networking, active collaboration and problem solving etc.
In addition, an Education Coordination Forum in Amman has been established with UNICEF as the coordinator, following the evacuation of international staff to Amman. This forum also meets on a fortnightly basis and brings together UN agencies and other partners, specially the NGOs, Donors etc. for purposes similar to the forum referred to above in Baghdad.
Regular thematic group meetings of interested partners around issues of common interest are being organised [example around the issue of standards for school furniture] and will be further strengthened during 2005.
Donor coordination meetings will also be regularly organised / attended to obtain synergy of action by UN with other partners.

Security scenario for planning purposes:
It is important to note that the above education sector plan has been developed with the assumption that during the year 2005, the security will continue to be in Phase-4 but will, thereafter improve to Phase- 3, following the January 30 elections.

Coordination Mechanisms and Programme Modalities:

Health Cluster coordination is undertaken on behalf of UN agencies operating, or planning to operate, in Iraq by WHO (‘Programme Support Team’) in Amman. The current Task Manager is Dr. Naeema Al Gasseer WHO/ WR, with the Cluster deputy being Dr. Alex Malyavin of UNICEF.  Active UN agencies in Health include WHO, UNICEF, UNFPA, WFP, UNDP, UNIDO, UNEP and IOM, with additional interest from UNIFEM and UNOPS. The is a large number of UN national technical staff active in Health in Iraq, including personnel associated with disease surveillance activities (with additional support staff in terms of security guards and others).

Regular contact is maintained between the UN agencies and with the World Bank, Ministries of Health, Environment, and Planning and with other health partners. WHO is playing an active, though restricted, role in the on-going national health planning process. Donor coordination remains for now, mostly bilateral, although MOH is planning to become more active in this area. Opportunities for local-level contacts are severely constrained by current UN Phase IV restrictions on in-country movement by national staff. National and international NGOs are currently engaged in activities in Iraq and through our weekly coordination meetings health cluster members exchange information with these counterparts. Any re-entry by international staff is likely to be under the auspices of the ‘Integrated Sectoral Approach’ which foresees a single point of entry into the UN system.

Weekly Cluster health coordination meetings (WHO)
Health Donors Coordination Committee (HDCC)
Participation in MOH National Health Plan Working Groups (WHO, UNICEF)

COORDINATION MECHANISMS AND PROGRAMME MODALITIES:
Task Manager: Annie Demirjian (UNDP), Deputy Task Manager: John Pace (UNAMI/HRO)

Task Manager:
UNDP is the Task Manager Agency for this cluster with UNAMI/HRO as Deputy.  Planning and implementation activities are co-ordinated within the cluster through bi-monthly meetings for cluster members. Peer group review of proposals, for submission to the Trust Fund, is conducted in smaller working groups, based on subject matter and areas of intervention. The Task Manager plays a key role in ensuring that all participating agencies and other participants are informed and consulted. The Task Manager may be asked to represent the interests of other agencies while meeting with counterparts including: Iraqi, international donor organizations, international NGOs and other government representatives.  A working group has reviewed the operating principles of Cluster 9 and has made some recommendations to improve project planning and implementation focus.
Implementation Modalities:
The implementation of projects requires close coordination and agreement of the Iraqi authorities and national civil society organizations. The national elections are a determining point in its history and it will have a direct impact on the implementation approach and methodology of Cluster activities.  In the absence of UN in Iraq, in the short term and to help develop local partnership, an Iraqi “Cluster Co-ordinator’ should be appointed to implement and monitor interventions.  Plans are underway to include regional partners, such as other Arab governments, research, training institutions and CSOs, NGOs. As well, Iraqi public and private sectors will act as executing and/or implementation agencies. The UN plan to operate in safer areas, such as Erbil and Basra, will be fully supported by UN.  UN will also rely on national capacity and absorption to implement and monitor programmes. Use TOKTEN expertise in project implementation. 
Inter-Agency Coordination:
Cluster 9 has moved towards a ‘Programme-Based Approach’ (PBA) planning and implementation modality. PBA approach underlines the strength of each UN agency while bringing under one Agency management the collaborative efforts of specialized agencies. The ‘ Human Rights Programme for Iraq’ and the ‘Media Development Programme’ are two PBA initiatives. The former spearheaded by UNAMI/HRO and the latter by UNESCO, combines wider consultation, planning and multi-year budgeting approach, with Iraqi counterparts and international donor community. PBA brings under one umbrella, short, medium and long term projects of relevant UN agencies while recognizing, the current security situation, hence focusing on capacity building and institutional strengthening interventions. The interventions include: joint strategic planning with Iraqi counterparts, capacity building activities, conferences, workshops and training to take place out side the country, as well as inside, should security situation improve.   All efforts will be made to engage national staff, NGOs and INGOs, including the private sector. In addition, other Iraqi implementation organizations will include consulting firms, academic and research institutions. 

Given the complexity of the issues and of the implementation challenges, focused co-ordination with other Clusters is paramount. Cluster 9 will maintain close co-ordination with other Clusters and in particular with the following Clusters:

Cluster 10 - Poverty Reduction and Human Development - All programmes and projects to be implemented in Iraq are fully aware of the human development needs and alleviation of poverty. Unemployment and the urgent need to generate jobs for the population at large and most importantly for youth and income generating opportunities for women will be incorporated in the capacity building and training programmes.  
Cluster 8 – IDPs and refugees - The return and reintegration of refugees and IDPs will have a major impact on the human capital of Iraq and for longer-term stabilization. The rights of the refugees and IDPs will be incorporated in all interventions working with key Ministries such as Human Rights, Justice and Displacement and Migration.
Co-ordination with Cluster 4 - Infrastructure and Housing - Decentralization and support to local governments, infrastructure and urban/rural policy development programmes are priority of the Iraqi Government as indicated in NDS. Capacity building, public policy development and programmes will be co-ordinated and implemented with Cluster 4.

Note: Constitutional and Support to Local Governments: The Cluster will co-ordinate with all UN agencies/Clusters and as well as UNAMI all activities supporting the Iraqi constitutional drafting process and strengthening the institutional and human resource capacities of local governments. 
Linkages with Iraqi Authorities and other actors:
Co-ordination mechanisms are in place with most national counterparts (both inside and outside Iraq National counterparts include ministries, local authorities, CSOs, academic & research institutions and the media.  In addition, Cluster 9’s role in Aid Management and Donor Co-ordination (management and database) will help provide the mechanisms to collect, compile and disseminate financial information and data through Ministry of Planning and Development Coordination (MoPDC), who, in turn, will share with the wider community.

Task manager: UNDP is the Task Manager Agency for this cluster with UNOPS as Deputy. Activities will be strongly coordinated within the cluster through regular information sharing mechanisms and meetings. The Task Manager will play a key role in ensuring that all participating agencies are informed and consulted, if need be, on on-going work. The Task Manager may be asked to represent the interests of other agencies while meeting with counterparts in Iraq. A working group has commenced to coordinate the various activities of this complex cluster.

Implementation Modalities:  Iraq is a country in conflict.  The current situation requires different implementation modalities than the UN employs in other development areas.  The implementation of the projects requires close coordination with and agreement of the Iraqi counterparts.  It should be accepted that there safe areas that the UN can operate in such as the north and the south, specifically Erbil and Basra.  The implementation of the projects also will utilize local Iraqi expertise.

Inter-Agency Coordination:
The programme is to be implemented both inside and outside of the country. All activities are planned in light of the current security context (Phase 4), with capacity building activities, conferences, workshops and partners negotiations will to take place outside the country. Direct support services will be initiated, if security permits, by the national staff, or will be outsourced to the private sector and local and international NGOs present in the country. The use of cascade training and training of trainers will be encouraged. Other activities for inside Iraq will use a variety of counterparts, such as NGOs, the Private Sector, in order to successfully implement and reduce UN visibility.

Activities will be strongly coordinated within the cluster through regular information sharing mechanisms and meetings. 
Coordination with Cluster 1 - Education and Culture
The rehabilitation of training and vocational centres will have a major impact on the human capital of Iraq and for long-term stabilisation. The various vulnerable groups of Iraq, the rural poor, IDPs, disabled etc, will also benefit from vocational training activities planned by the Education Cluster. Representatives of both Clusters will meet to coordinate these activities.

Coordination with Cluster 5 - Agriculture, Water Resources and Environment and Cluster 6 - Food Security.
The cluster is working closely with other relevant clusters namely Cluster 6: Food Security and Cluster 5: Agriculture, Water Resources and Environment, in relation to poverty reduction and safety net. The current collaboration with WB and Food security cluster will result in some input related to Market direction and capacity. Moreover, WFP's Household study covering 31,000 households has provided among other elements the coping strategy followed by the vulnerable population. The combined efforts will lead to determination of the safety net strategy and aspects of economic development. On the other hand Agriculture and Water Resources cluster is looking into rural under-employment and increasing level of agriculture production paving the way to a better rural economy and its interaction with macro food market.

Coordination with Cluster 8 - IDPs and Refugees.
The return and reintegration of refugees and IDPs will have a major impact on the human capital of Iraq and for long-term stabilization. As some of the most vulnerable groups in Iraq, refugees, IDPs and returnees will benefit from employment programmes and income generation activities planned by the cluster on Poverty Reduction and Human Development.

·     Coordination with Cluster 9 – Governance and Civil Society
       Cluster 10 will work closely with Cluster 9 on issues concerned with capacity building, training, studies related to regulatory    activities, the setting up of the Management Training Institute and the Human Development Centre.

Cross-Cutting issues:
All programme and projects to be implemented in Iraq are fully aware of the needs of human rights, gender and environment needs within planning and have incorporated them throughout the initiatives. 

Note: Employment as a Cross-Cutting Issue: 
This cluster shall promote the use of appropriate labour-based employment throughout all the work of the UN. The importance of employment and income generation in the restoration of Iraqi living standards will continue to be essential. To this effect, Cluster 10 will regularly integrate the recommendations from the ILO action plan on employment which was endorsed in December 2004.
